summary: Describes an RTP header extension that conveys information about video frames needed for error recovery and packet forwarding in middleboxes. It helps when media is encrypted and middleboxes lack keys. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: A box handler can't open parcels but can read stickers on them. These stickers tell it which video pieces matter.

subtitle: Tell RTP switches about video frames without decrypting the video.

tldr.problem: RTP switches need information about video frames (keyframes, layer structure, etc.) to forward encrypted video, but SRTP encryption hides this metadata in the payload.
tldr.mechanism: A video frame marking RTP header extension carries critical metadata (frame type, discardability, layer IDs) outside the encrypted payload, allowing codec-agnostic processing without decryption.
tldr.outcome: RTP switches can selectively forward video layers and switch on keyframes without decrypting media, improving both quality and performance for encrypted video conferencing.

facts.label: Extension header length
facts.value: 1, 2, or 3 octets depending on fields present

today: RFC 9626 is an experimental specification published in March 2025. It provides mechanisms for RTP switches to process encrypted video streams without decryption keys, enabling secure video forwarding in conferencing systems. The specification is under evaluation for broader adoption in video communication standards.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Modern video conferencing systems use RTP switches to select and forward streams from participants. A switch needs critical metadata about video frames to make good forwarding decisions: where frames can be switched (intra-frames), which frames can be dropped without affecting quality, and which layers of scalable video to forward. However, Secure RTP (SRTP) encrypts the payload, hiding this metadata from switches and middleboxes.

The video frame marking RTP header extension solves this by carrying essential metadata outside the encrypted payload. This allows switches to make codec-agnostic forwarding decisions without decryption keys, and enables forwarding of encrypted end-to-end media where the switch has no keys at all.
sections.plainLanguage: The video is locked in a box that only the receiver can open. But a sticker on the box tells the switch helpful information: is this a keyframe, can it be dropped, what layer is it in.

sections.title: RTP Header Extension Format
sections.content:
The extension is defined in two main formats: a long form for scalable streams and a short form for non-scalable streams. Both use RFC 8285 one-byte or two-byte header extension format. The extension carries six key bits:

S (Start of Frame) is 1 in the first packet of a frame. E (End of Frame) is 1 in the last packet. I (Independent Frame) is 1 for intra-frames (e.g., H.264 IDR) that can be decoded without prior frames. D (Discardable Frame) is 1 if the frame can be dropped without breaking decodability. B (Base Layer Sync) is 1 for enhancement layers that only depend on the base temporal layer. TID (Temporal-layer ID) identifies the temporal layer (0 = base, higher = higher temporal fidelity). The long form also carries LID (Layer ID) for spatial and quality layers, and TL0PICIDX, a reference to the base layer picture index for dependency tracking.
sections.plainLanguage: The sticker lists: is this the start/end of a video chunk, can it stand alone, is it safe to throw away, what quality is it, and which older chunk does it depend on.

sections.title: Codec-Specific Mappings
sections.content:
Different video codecs encode scalability information differently. The specification maps codec-specific layer and frame information to the generic TID and LID fields, enabling a single header extension to work across multiple codecs. VP9 maps its 3-bit Spatial ID to LID and 3-bit Temporal ID to TID. H.265 uses 6-bit layer ID and 3-bit Temporal ID. H.264 Scalable Video Coding (SVC) encodes spatial layer (DID), quality layer (QID), and temporal layer separately. H.264 AVC and VP8 carry only temporal information.

This codec-agnostic approach lets switches make forwarding decisions without knowing which codec is in use. The specification provides detailed mapping rules so implementers can extract the correct bits from each codec's native layer information and populate the header extension accurately.
sections.plainLanguage: Different video cameras label their quality layers differently. This sticker translates all the different labels into one standard format that everyone understands.

sections.title: Usage and Forwarding Decisions
sections.content:
RTP switches use the frame marking extension to make three main decisions. First, when to switch streams: switches should select the first packet with the I bit set in all spatial layers to avoid showing a broken frame to users. Second, when to drop frames during congestion: drop frames marked with D bit set (discardable), or frames with the highest TID and LID values, which are typically less critical. Third, which layers to forward: based on TID and LID, switches can select subsets of layers for receivers with limited bandwidth or decoder capabilities.

The specification recommends using the frame marking extension only for temporally nested scalability structures (where each layer only depends on lower layers), not for complex irregular structures. Senders MUST ensure the header extension accurately reflects the actual frame properties; it is not meant for signaling or hints but for factual metadata already present in the media.
sections.plainLanguage: The switch reads the stickers to decide: is this a good place to switch to a new speaker, can I throw this chunk away to save bandwidth, and should I send all the quality layers or just the basic one.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
In SRTP, header extensions can be authenticated and optionally encrypted separately from the payload. When using the video frame marking extension, endpoints must decide whether to encrypt it. If unencrypted, the extension metadata is visible to all middleboxes on the network path. If encrypted, only SRTP peers (RTP switches) can read it.

Endpoints should balance privacy against functionality. For example, unencrypted metadata reveals keyframe frequency, which can be inferred from encrypted data through traffic analysis (keyframes are usually larger), but unencrypted metadata provides a reliable signal. The key consideration is that RTP switches are SRTP peers with access to encryption keys, whereas other middleboxes have no access to encrypted payload or encrypted extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: The sticker can be sealed (only the switch reads it) or visible (everyone on the network path can see it). If it is visible, people might guess from the stickers how the video is structured, but the actual video stays secret.
